newsitem.title: UK: YEAREND - UK equities weigh up life under Labour.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - UK equities weigh up life under Labour.

text.p: It has been a long time since the British stock market has had to live with a Labour Party government and its memories of the dying days of the last one are coloured by thoughts of high inflation and strikes.
Now, after 17 years of Conservative Party rule, opinion polls suggest Labour's Tony Blair is likely to lead his party to victory in an election which must be held by May 1997.
Investors have been busy trying to analyse the implications.
Ironically, despite the market's knee-jerk antipathy towards a Labour administration, there are historic precedents for the stock market to perform well under Labour.

Between Harold Wilson's Labour victory of October 1974, for instance, and the election of the Conservatives under Margaret Thatcher in May 1979, the FT-All Share index quadrupled in value from just above 60 to over 280.

And after an earlier e Wilson government devalued the currency in early 1967, the index leapt from around 95 to end the year at around 120. By contrast the bear market of 1973 and 1974 mostly occurred under the Conservative government of Edward Heath.
Such raw figures however can be misleading, since they take no account of inflation or of the market's relative performance compared with other leading markets.
LABOUR PARTY HAS MOVED ON

Anyway the world, and the Labour party, has changed a lot since the late 70s. Blair and his shadow finance minister Gordon Brown have worked hard to present a business-friendly front designed in part to keep the markets on their side.
In particular "New Labour" has hinted that it will stick to the Conservatives' 2-1/2 percent inflation target and has said it will keep borrowing and taxes under control.
Whether Labour proves true to its promise remains to be seen, and much policy detail remains to be spelt out.

"Economic policies seem sane but it is so long since Labour was in power and that increases the uncertainty," said Ian Williams, strategist at Panmure Gordon. "All the talk could be irrelevant when they are in power."

Worries over Labour policies, as well as the precise timing of the poll, have already overshadowed the market for some months -- one reason the FTSE 100 has underperformed other leading indexes this year.

"I would say the election is important because it provides event risk," said Richard Davidson, equity strategist at Morgan Stanley. "It could provide a shock, it could provide a change in policy, but everything tangible has been priced in."
ECONOMIC POLICY THE KEY, ALONG WITH SPECIFIC ISSUES
For the equity market the central issue is likely to be Labour's overall handling of the economy and it is here that a key test is likely to come in the weeks after the election.
With economic growth poised to increase through 1997 while government debt remains high, whoever is elected may be faced with tough decisions to raise taxes and interest rates.

There are specific areas of tax policy too that could have a significant bearing on shares. Most obviously Labour is expected to introduce a multi-billion pound "windfall" tax on privatised utilities, designed to finance training and employment measures.

The party is expected to take a tougher line on takeovers, breaking the free market philosophy of recent years that has helped return billions of pounds for investment funds to reinvest in the market.
Another possibility is that the party will introduce new shareholding rules to discourage over-active trading by investment funds in favour of long-term investment.
Yet some analysts believe the market will ride out any pre-election nerves.
"My inclination is that if the market starts to get jumpy ahead of the election, if it overreacts in one way it will probably go the other way in the aftermath," said Williams at Panmure.
